content: The Jimmy Fund is a Boston-based charity that supports cancer care and research at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Established in 1948, it initially focused on raising funds to combat childhood cancer but has since expanded its mission to include research and treatment for both adult and pediatric cancers. By 2006, the Jimmy Fund had raised over $500 million. The charity was launched with the help of the Variety Club of New England, now known as the Variety Children’s Charity of New England. Its inception involved a radio broadcast featuring a young cancer patient, nicknamed Jimmy, who was visited by members of the Boston Braves baseball team. Donations from listeners were used to buy Jimmy a television set so he could watch his favorite team play. This campaign raised over $200,000 in its first year, funding Dr. Sidney Farber’s groundbreaking cancer research and establishing the Jimmy Fund. Einar Gustafson, the original Jimmy, became an inspirational figure for the charity. In 1948, at the age of 12, he was a patient of Dr. Sidney Farber, a pioneer in modern chemotherapy and founder of the Children’s Cancer Research Foundation, which later became the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Gustafson, whose privacy was protected by the pseudonym Jimmy, expressed a desire for a television to watch the Boston Braves. His story was shared on Ralph Edwards' national radio program, Truth or Consequences, which was broadcast from his hospital room. The broadcast featured Braves players and ended with a plea for donations, leading to the birth of the Jimmy Fund. After his cancer went into remission, Gustafson returned to his family’s farm in Maine and later lived in Massachusetts. For decades, his identity remained unknown, and many assumed he had passed away due to the low survival rates of pediatric cancers at the time. However, in 1998, during the 50th anniversary of the original broadcast, Gustafson revealed himself as Jimmy. He became actively involved in the charity, recording public service announcements, visiting patients, and participating in events like the Pan-Massachusetts Challenge and the Boston Marathon Jimmy Fund Walk. Gustafson passed away in 2001 at the age of 65. The Jimmy Fund is closely affiliated with the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, one of the world’s leading centers for cancer care and research. The Jimmy Fund serves as a major fundraising arm for the institute, which is recognized by the National Cancer Institute for its contributions to oncology. The Jimmy Fund Clinic, a premier center for pediatric cancer research and treatment, was instrumental in achieving the first-ever remissions of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia through drug therapy. The clinic is designed to be child-friendly, featuring Disney-themed decorations and playrooms, creating a welcoming environment for young patients. The Boston Red Sox have maintained a longstanding partnership with the Jimmy Fund since 1953, making it the longest and most significant team-charity relationship in professional sports. The partnership is celebrated annually, often coinciding with the Red Sox home opener, and includes events like Jimmy Fund Day at Fenway Park and an 18-hour radio-telethon in collaboration with WEEI and NESN. Ted Williams, a legendary Red Sox player, was a key figure in promoting the Jimmy Fund. He worked closely with Dr. Sidney Farber to raise awareness and funds for cancer research, often visiting children in hospitals and participating in fundraising events without seeking publicity. Williams’ efforts helped establish the Jimmy Fund as a prominent charity. Mike Andrews, a former Red Sox second baseman, has served as chairman of the Jimmy Fund for over 25 years. His involvement began during his rookie season in 1967 when he visited a patient at the request of Bill Koster, the then-chairman of the Jimmy Fund. After retiring from baseball, Andrews dedicated himself to the charity full-time and has been instrumental in its growth and success. Several organizations have played significant roles in supporting the Jimmy Fund. The Massachusetts Chiefs of Police Association adopted the Jimmy Fund as their official charity in 1953, organizing events like softball games and picnics to raise funds. The Variety Children’s Charity of New England was pivotal in the creation of the Jimmy Fund, raising $45,000 in its first fundraising drive in 1947 to support Dr. Farber’s research. Hollywood stars such as John Wayne, Dean Martin, and Frank Sinatra also contributed their time and influence to the cause. The Jimmy Fund organizes numerous fundraising events, including the Boston Marathon Jimmy Fund Walk, which allows participants to walk the historic marathon route in honor or memory of loved ones affected by cancer. The Pan-Massachusetts Challenge, a fundraising bike-a-thon, generates nearly 50% of the Jimmy Fund’s annual revenue and is its largest contributor. Other events include the Jimmy Fund Golf program, which has raised over $53 million since 1983, and the Jimmy Fund Scooper Bowl, the nation’s largest all-you-can-eat ice cream festival. The Jimmy Fund/Variety Children’s Charity Theater Program, established in 1949, involves participating movie theaters showing short films about Dana-Farber’s work and collecting donations from audiences. John Hancock Fantasy Day at Fenway Park offers baseball fans the opportunity to play on the iconic field while supporting the Jimmy Fund. The Walk and Rock for the Jimmy Fund, organized by Worcester Academy students, features walk-a-thons and a Battle of the Bands, with proceeds supporting adolescent and young adult cancer programs at Dana-Farber. The WEEI/NESN Jimmy Fund Radio-Telethon is an annual two-day event featuring celebrity guests, patient stories, and calls from donors. Since its inception in 2002, it has raised approximately $12 million for the Jimmy Fund. Burger King has also supported the charity since 2000 through its Chance for Kids scratch ticket campaign, which has expanded across New England and neighboring states, raising millions for the cause.
